title: Sadako and the Thousand Paper Cranes
author: Eleanor Coerr
target_audience: Educators teaching about Hiroshima, World War II, and peace
Readers interested in real-life stories of courage
Families seeking educational and inspirational books
core_themes: The effects of war on children
Hope in the face of adversity
Symbolism of the origami crane and peace
primary_purpose: To share the true story of Sadako Sasaki, a young Japanese girl who became a symbol of hope, peace, and resilience after being affected by the Hiroshima atomic bomb, and to inspire readers to seek peace and understanding in a world touched by conflict.

structure_format.narrative_style: Third-person narrative, accessible and sensitive, uses evocative and simple language appropriate for children
structure_format.organization: Divided into short chapters following Sadako’s life from her childhood in Hiroshima, her diagnosis with leukemia, her determination to fold a thousand paper cranes, and ultimately her legacy
features: Includes historical context of Hiroshima bombing
Features afterword and photographs in some editions

key_concepts_lessons: The personal cost of warfare and nuclear weapons, especially on innocent civilians.
Resilience and finding hope through small acts, represented by folding paper cranes.
The importance of family, friendship, and community support during times of hardship.
The power of individual actions to inspire broader movements for peace.
The role of memory and memorial in healing and promoting peace.
notable_features: True story of a child affected by the Hiroshima bomb and subsequent leukemia
Popular in peace education and anti-war teaching worldwide
Emphasizes Japanese culture (especially origami and traditional customs)
Includes photographs or illustrations to enhance educational value in some editions
Frequently used in schools to discuss topics of war, peace, and hope
cultural_historical_context: Set and written in the shadow of the Hiroshima atomic bombing (August 6, 1945), this book brought international attention to the civilian suffering caused by nuclear warfare and helped spread the symbolism of the paper crane as a sign of peace. The book contributed to the worldwide peace movement and has been translated into many languages.
reception_impact: Widely acclaimed as a children’s classic and important work for peace education
Used in schools and libraries globally to discuss themes of war and peace
Helped establish Sadako’s story as a universal symbol of peace for children and adults alike
Inspired global memorials and annual paper crane projects
Noted by some critics for simplification of historical context, but praised for its emotional impact and accessibility
comparable_titles: Hiroshima No Pika by Toshi Maruki
The Big Wave by Pearl S. Buck
Year of the Boar and Jackie Robinson by Bette Bao Lord (for multicultural and historical children's narratives)
